## A source is evidence, not just notes

Every transcription starts with a piece of music. It also starts with a
decision about evidence: which score or recording you actually heard, how to
find it again, and what its terms let you do with it. Leave that paperwork
until after the notes are typed and you'll pay for it twice: once when two
editions disagree about measure 7, and again when you want to share an
arrangement and can't say where the original came from.

Different libraries need different care. IMSLP holds scans and editions whose
legal status varies item by item and country by country. Mutopia publishes
typeset scores with terms displayed alongside each one. MuseScore hosts
community uploads, so being able to open a page settles nothing about the
rights attached to it. *Public domain* is a legal status, not a synonym for old
music. A composition can be free of copyright while the engraving, translation,
performance, or arrangement in front of you is still protected.

What you want is a small source record living beside the score data: title,
composer, edition or arranger, repository, stable page address, the displayed
licence statement, the date you looked, and the bars you plan to transcribe.
That record isn't decoration wrapped around the music. It's your route back to
the evidence when a pitch, a measure number, or a permission needs checking.

## Play it, then read what's missing

This program keeps the source description and a first audition in one object.
Its seven-note phrase is invented, which avoids making any claim about a named
edition while the fields are still placeholders. Notice the metadata can be
incomplete without stopping playback. That's exactly why the log prints the
gaps where you can't miss them.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84
use_synth :piano

candidate = {
  title: "Practice candidate",
  repository: "replace with the source collection",
  licence: "copy the exact statement from the source page",
  accessed: "YYYY-MM-DD",
  bars: "1-4",
  notes: [:c4, :d4, :e4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :c4],
  durations: [0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 2]
}

candidate[:notes].zip(candidate[:durations]).each do |note_name, duration|
  play note_name, release: duration * 0.8
  sleep duration
end

puts "Source: #{candidate[:repository]}"
puts "Licence note: #{candidate[:licence]}"
```

The phrase climbs from C to G and comes home, and the long final C settles it.
Meanwhile the log shows you an unfinished repository and an unfinished licence.
Music plays; the candidate isn't ready to become anything you can share.
Keeping both facts in view stops a pleasant audition from outrunning the source
work behind it.

## Fill in the real fields

1. Replace the repository and licence strings with the wording from one actual
   candidate page. Copy it, don't paraphrase it. Run the phrase again and read
   the log as if a stranger had sent it to you. Could you find that exact page
   from what it says?
2. Replace the invented notes and durations with one complete phrase from a
   candidate whose stated terms fit what you intend to do. Keep the bar range
   with the data. Stop at the end of the phrase, not at the end of four
   measures: a cut through a cadence leaves the extract sounding interrupted.
3. Add an edition or arranger field. When the page gives neither, write
   `"not stated"`. Playback doesn't change at all, and that's the point.
   Provenance can improve while nothing audible moves.

## Bytes never carry their own permissions

You already know values whose handling depends on metadata travelling beside
them. A file's bytes can't tell you whether you're allowed to redistribute
them, and identical bytes arrive under different terms all the time. Pitches
have the same limitation. Two pages can carry the same composition while the
scan, engraving, editorial additions, and arrangement on each sit in different
legal positions.

Provenance pays off in musical debugging too. Suppose measure 7 sounds wrong a
week after you typed it. With a source record you reopen the exact artefact and
compare the event against a fixed coordinate. Without one, even "measure 7" is
ambiguous, because another edition counts the pickup differently, renumbers a
section, or prints a variant reading. The edition field is often the whole
explanation for why two careful transcriptions disagree.

Building a shortlist surfaces these differences early. Twenty candidates is
enough to compare range, texture, score clarity, recording availability, and
displayed terms. For a first ear transcription, pick a clear monophonic line
where you can hear individual attacks. For score entry, pick readable engraving
and stable measure numbers, so the only hard questions are the musical ones.

None of this is legal advice. Copyright duration and public-domain rules depend
on jurisdiction, and a composer's death date settles nothing about a given
edition or recording. When a page is unclear, either choose a source that
states its terms explicitly or get advice suited to where and how you plan to
publish.

## Twenty candidates, three choices

Create `sources.md` and describe twenty candidates. For each one, record a
stable page address, the displayed licence or public-domain statement, the date
you accessed it, the named edition or arranger, rough difficulty, texture, and
a proposed bar range. Then cut the list to three: one melody to transcribe by
ear, one score for exact entry, and one larger capstone candidate.

Write the entries so another reader can recover every source and see why each
extract is musically workable, without having to ask which version you meant.
[Lesson 43](43-four-pass-pipeline.qmd) puts the first of those three through a four-pass pipeline, and the
bar range you chose becomes the excerpt.
